subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ANY AGREEMENTS MADE AT BUSINESS-LABOUR MEETING TO RESTRAIN DEMANDS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from comments of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) made outside this House that, and I quote:
. . . there is a real desire growing and permeating through labour that it will exercise proper restraint in the post-control period .. . union leaders can persuade workers to exercise restraint.
Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada said he would not lift controls before the end of 1978 because, and I quote:
To the extent that groups in the economy are in fact looking to the ending of controls as the moment for a substantial upward push in their money incomes and prices . ..
Because there are open rumours that no agreement on restraint was made between business and labour at the meeting a week ago, which fact is reflected in recent editorials, and yet today's press quotes of the Minister of Labour would lead to the conclusion that labour is in fact committed to restraint, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That this House direct the Minister of Labour to make a statement forthwith in this House advising all hon. members and the public of Canada just exactly what was agreed to at the business-labour meeting and specifically whether the statements of the Minister of Labour that labour has a real desire to exercise proper restraint is an accurate reflection of any agreement made at the meeting or accurately reflects any commitment made directly to the government by the Canadian Labour Congress Leaders.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF WAGE EARNERS BE DEDUCTIBLE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion of pressing necessity.
Considering that, except for some allowances, the Income Tax Act does not entitle most wage earners to ask for a reduction of more than 3 per cent of employment income, up to a maximum of $150, while they have to pay from $300 to $600 yearly to travel to and from their place of employment; considering that there would be great opportunities to save a considerable amount of energy if most wage earners or workers generally were prompted to use public transport to go to work and that anyhow the various levels of government must pay subsidies worth several million dollars, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That the House instruct the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) to bring in as soon as possible an amendment to section 8(I)(a) to the Income Tax Act to the effect that travelling expenses to and from the place of employment made by wage earners using public transportation be deductible from their income for income tax purposes upon the filing of receipts and records.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may respond to the question. I think I must make the observation with regard to the analysis tabled last Friday by the Quebec ministers that it involved conclusions which are hardly supported by the study which was tabled at the same time. For example, it was clear that the general costs of overhead of the government of Canada which include, of course, the benefits received by the people of Quebec were not included in the balance sheet which the Quebec ministers drew up. With regard to the figures of fiscal transfers, the revenue figures of the government of Canada from various elements of taxation and also with regard to their expenditures, let me say
Oral Questions
that these are now in the public accounts of Canada and can be examined by the Quebec members and indeed by other interested persons.
A far more difficult question and the one requiring far more analysis is the extent to which one can take, for example, the distribution of interest, of dividends, of public expenditures and facilities, and the various other distribution effects of the government of Canada and break them down on a province by province basis. These are expenditures and costs which are not normally kept on this basis and require very considerable judgment. Some attention is being given to that question, but it is not a question, as I think will become increasingly clear from a close analysis of taxation, with respect to which one could rush in and make hasty conclusions without careful analysis.

maintopic: JUSTIFICATION FOR EXPENDITURES ON INTERNATIONAL COMPETITIONS AT EXPENSE OF LOCAL AMATEUR SPORTS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that question has been discussed at length during two sittings of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, last Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, if my memory serves me right. The officials who appeared before the committee have explained the reasons which could warrant either position, that is to protect the owners of small trawlers which cannot go in the gulf outside zones and thus depend, for at least 95 per cent of their catches, on the health of stocks inside the gulf. subsubtopic: TANKER TRAFFIC ALONG WESTERN COAST OF CANADA
speechtext: What (a) installations (b) services to control tanker traffic along the western coast of Canada (i) exist (ii) are planned?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: TANKER TRAFFIC ALONG WESTERN COAST OF CANADA
speechtext:
(a) (i) Existing installations: The major facility for control of tanker traffic on the west coast of Canada comprises the vessel traffic management centre located in the Capilano 100 building, West Vancouver. This Centre is equipped with radar, closed-circuit television and extensive communications facilities including dedicated communications links for the exchange of information with the United States Coast Guard Centre at Seattle, (b) (i) Existing Services: The Centre previously described manages the Vancouver traffic zone which includes Canadian waters in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Haro Strait and the area between Vancouver Island and the Canadian mainland. Participation is voluntary at present and operating procedures are fully described for the information of mariners in the "Annual Edition of Notices to Mariners". The zone is divided into four sectors, operated as follows: Sector One (Strait of Juan de Fuca): Ship shore communication facilities enable participating ships to communicate with Vancouver traffic centre, advising the centre of their locations and intended movements and receiving information concerning other traffic in the vicinity as well as weather and navigational hazards. A voluntary communications service, operated by the United States coast
[Mr. Whelan.)

guard, is also available in this sector. Sector Two (Haro Strait and waters east of Vancouver Island): Service in this sector is identical to that provided in sector one, with the exception of the United States operated communications system. Sector Three (Vancouver Harbour and Approaches): Radar equipment, supplemented by closed circuit television, enables the centre to monitor traffic in English Bay, the approaches to Vancouver Harbour and the Harbour itself. Ship shore communication facilities are also provided, as in Sectors One and Two. Sector Four (Fraser River-South Arm): Commencing March 1, 1977, Vancouver traffic zone is extended into the south arm of the Fraser River. Facilities in this sector are limited to a system of bridge to bridge communication, with vessels advising each other of their presence when passing specified calling in points. Tofino Traffic Zone and Prince Rupert Traffic Zone provide an extension of vessel traffic management services into the western and northern waters of British Columbia respectively. Participation is voluntary at present and is based upon each ship transmitting a message giving certain basic navigation information at critical points during her passage to all other participating vessels in the immediate area. As a means of enhancing navigation safety in the Strait of Juan de Fuca and the Strait of Georgia, voluntary traffic routing systems have been established in these areas. If it is determined that the systems are effective in promoting navigation safety, they will be considered for mandatory use. A medium frequency radiotelephone ship to ship and ship shore traffic monitoring and regulating system operates in the Mackenzie river to prevent congestion in constricted and dangerous areas. It also provides navigation safety information and weather forecasts and is conducted through Canadian coast guard radio stations.
(a) (ii)Installations Planned: Facilities presently under construction, and expected to be in operation during 1977 include: Tofino Traffic Centre: By means of long-range radar and radio facilities, this centre will be able to monitor, and communicate with, traffic approaching and departing from the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Vancouver Traffic Centre: Remote controlled radar installations mounted at strategic locations will provide surveillance of traffic in Haro Strait and the southern part of the Strait of Georgia. A radio direction-finding system will enable the Vancouver Centre to make a positive identification of vessels in this area, (b) (ii) Services Planned: Coupled with the provision of extended surveillance and identification equipment, it is intended to make participation in the Vancouver and Tofino Traffic Zones compulsory, thus providing active control over marine traffic in these areas. Extension of the present service in the Prince Rupert zone is also anticipated, but details of the degree and type of service to be provided will
not be decided until a decision has been reached on the proposed Kitimat project.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
that the Second Report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, presented to the House on Thursday, February 3, 1977 be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, most of the legislation that has cleared this chamber these days and in recent years has contained provisions whereby the governor in council, the minister or some agency may make regulations for carrying out of the purposes of the legislation that we pass. The question arises as to how this process is carried out; whether there is ever an attempt to see that the process is carried out in the spirit of the original legislation and, if not, what sort of remedies are available. It is to these three important questions that I address myself this afternoon.
The scrutiny of what one might call the delegated parliament, as opposed to the parliament in which we sit, owes its existence to several outstanding figures in this House. I think credit is due all around this chamber, but I would single out
March 28, 1977

the hon. member for Peace River, who seconded my motion for concurrence, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville, on the other side, who is chairman of the committee that brought in very important recommendations in this field, the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Bonaventure-!les-de-la-Madeleine, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council, the hon. member for Regina East, and the deputy House leader of the Conservative party. These are several of the prominent figures, but there are more besides. When one mentions some names, the danger is that one does not mention nearly enough. In any event, people such as Senators Forsey, Godfrey, Lafond, Yuzyk and others made substantial contributions in this particular field. At the beginning of this parliament I had the honour to be chosen, with Senator Forsey, as joint chairman of the committee. I succeeded the hon. member for Fundy-Royal. That shows that my stricture about myself was worth-while, since I had neglected to mention his name. He was a tall figure in this field, both physically and otherwise.
From the beginning of this parliament the work of this committee has continued and has culminated in the report, concurrence in which I have now moved. It is one of the lengthiest reports ever presented by a joint parliamentary committee. It is presented in a specially printed form covering 57 pages of two columns each. It includes a large variety of points, some technical, others simplicity itself. I shall review the work of the committee and deal with some of the recommendations I consider as particularly important, and then listen to the hon. member for Peace River, the Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Greenwood, and perhaps the parliamentary secretary to the President of the Privy Council comment on the work of this committee.
Sometimes those of us working in special committees think our committee is a world of its own and we wonder how the work will fare when it is scrutinized by this House. This afternoon and this evening, no doubt, I shall have my share of elation when others review the work of the committee, and perhaps my share of regret that we did not do better in certain respects.
I now come to the report itself. It covers the work of the committee from January 1, 1974, until January 27, 1977. For those who are not familiar with the workings of the committee, let me say that its work is initiated-I think that is putting it correctly-by two counsel to the committee, Mr. E. G. Egling-ton and Miss Lise Mayrand, and their efficient secretary, Mrs. Helen Leroux. They look at all the regulations, statutory instruments, and the like, of the various ministries and Crown emanations. Then, having scrutinized this vast body of regulations, our counsel come before the committee and report whether they see any irregularities in them or any other points which ought to be followed up. Paragraph 3 of the report perhaps best describes the work of the committee. It reads in part:
The committee's primary function is to maintain a watch on the subordinate law made by delegates of parliament. In the modern era parliament has been forced
Statutory Instruments
by considerations of time and lack of technical and scientific expertise to leave to subordinates the making of detailed rules and regulations and to confine itself increasingly to setting the main structures of legislative interventions in society. However, parliament retains responsibility for the law of the land and to the extent that those detailed rules and regulations are not subject to parliamentary scrutiny, parliament is forfeiting its effective right to settle the laws that must be obeyed by the people.
Later in my speech I shall draw an important distinction between the work of parliament and what parliament can do and the work of the committee and what the committee cannot do. I draw a tantalizing curtain over that part of my speech by simply saying that it is possible for one of those two bodies to order a cook to be boiled in oil. If hon. members listen, they will learn later in my speech whether parliament or the delegated authority is able to order such an awesome punishment. I mention some figures. I point out that we are a continuing committee. Every week we deal with several dozen regulations, orders in council, statutory instruments, and the like. Up to July 15 last year the committee dealt with 1,348 instruments, which represents a massive amount of work. About half those instruments passed the committee without commentary, but after having been scrutinized by our counsel. Questions arose about the other half. Many of those questions were minor, although some were of substantial nature.
In the report presented to the House we have drawn attention to what we regard as defects in particular instruments. It is not likely that the committee will again make such a lengthy report to the House. I think we will be more apt to look into particular instances which concern us. That is a fair summation of the committee's work. For example, we are currently looking at the method by which increases in first-class postage were brought about by the use of a section in the Financial Administration Act rather than by an amendment to the Post Office Act. No doubt in due course the House will discover our findings in that regard.
A couple of years ago, in 1974, both Houses adopted criteria for the examination of statutory instruments. Those criteria were really an elaboration on the smaller number of criteria set forth in our founding legislation, the Statutory Instruments Act. There are some 16 or 17 criteria about which we are concerned. Perhaps I may refer to four or five of those criteria to make my remarks clearer. The criteria are found in paragraph 10 of part B of the report. We look at a statutory instrument or regulation to determine if, in our judgment it, and I quote criterion (1 )(b)-
does not clearly state therein the precise authority for the making of the instrument.
In one half of the committee's work, whether to do with the Privy Council office with which we were most directly dealing, or the various ministries, that criterion was referred to many times, for it is a generally accepted practice in the government that when statutory instruments are framed, the precise authority for the making of the instrument must be clearly stated. We found that the occasions for invoking criterion (l)(b) were few. In this regard, I think the committee would like to commend publicly-as I am doing in this debate-the

March 28, 1977
Statutory Instruments
ministry for its co-operation. The second criterion is number 4, that the regulation or other statutory instrument-
makes some unusual or unexpected use of the powers conferred by the enabling statute or by the prerogative-
Here I will refer to what I call the Baby-face Nelson amendment. It was once put out under the Explosives Act. The problem and the reason for the objection by the committee is that section 108.1(2) of the regulations prohibits the sale of fireworks to a person who appears to be under the age of 18 years. In their wisdom, the committee considered that the subsection could be given effect to in this wise even if you are under the age of 18 years: if you appear to be under 18, you may not buy fireworks. This is not the most earthshaking problem that has ever been encountered. We took it up with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which agreed with the committee that the subsection should be replaced by better wording. 1 hope that the Baby-face Nelson amendment has now been put to rest, because the department came forth with these words:
No person shall sell any fireworks to a person who appears to be under the age of 18 years and does not produce evidence that he is of the age of 18 years or over.
The third criteria I go to is number 9, whether any regulation or other statutory instrument, and I quotein the absence of express authority to that effect in the enabling statute or prerogative, appears to amount to the exercise of a substantive legislative power properly the subject of direct parliamentary enactment, and not merely to the formulation of subordinate provisions of a technical or administrative character properly the subject of delegated legislation-
Here one is in the very important field of the question of whether the delegated act or instrument, in effect, amounts to the making of policy rather than to carrying out the purposes of the legislation. This is something that strikes right home at ourselves as members of parliament because under the representational gifts remission order it states:
-"in recognition of international comity and practice that heads of state, heads of government, ministerial representatives of government and members of parliament exchange gifts during official visits" customs duty, sales tax and excise tax shall be remitted on gifts received by the prime minister, ministers, and members of parliament on official visits to other countries or presented by visiting foreign donors in Canada.
The committee considered these remission orders very carefully. It was of the opinion that they were not concerned with administrative detail but constituted a substantive departure from established taxation law, giving us, in effect, a special privilege. That is set forth in the report. This reminds me of the time I headed a delegation of parliamentarians to Finland. One of the more splendid gifts of the Finnish parliament was a 40-ounce bottle of Finnish vodka which found itself in my luggage when I arrived back at the Halifax international airport. I was able to persuade Customs that I had accepted this 40-ounce bottle in trust on behalf of the parliament of Canada and that I would be able to share my pleasure with my fellow parliamentarians. I take the opportunity now of saying it was a great pleasure indeed.

speechtext: Did you share it?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The spirit of the pleasure I shared if not the spirit itself. In any event, if you look at the report and examine the front portion of it, you will find that the representational gifts remission order came under some consideration by the members of the committee. The fourth example, criterion number 10, provides that whether any regulation or statutory instrument, and I quotewithout express provision to the effect having been made in the enabling statute or prerogative, imposes a fine, imprisonment or other penalty, or shifts the onus of proof of innocence to the person accused of an offence-
Members will be reassured to know that this criterion has never had to be invoked. We have never got into the field so far that fines, imprisonment or other penalties arose by administrative act rather than by the express provision in an enabling statute. Finally, in dealing with these 17 criteria may I point out criterion number 5, a very important one that we looked at on a very large number of occasions namely, whether any regulation or other statutory instrument-
-(a) tends directly or indirectly to exclude the jurisdiction of the courts without explicit authorization therefor in the enabling statute; or
(b) makes the rights and liberties of the subject dependent on administrative discretion rather than on the judicial process-
A sample that I will quote in this regard deals with the sale of postage stamps and their regulations. I quote from the report:
Section 14 of these regulations gives to any postmaster an unfettered power to cancel any licence at any time issued under the regulations.
A corner grocery store with a postage stamp vending machine may suddenly lose that if the local postmaster decides that it should. The committee was concerned by the fact that no grounds or criteria are spelled out as justifying cancellation. There is no provision for a hearing or any opportunity for the licensee to be heard, or any obligation to tell the licensee why he is losing that particular right. The Minister of Justice may argue, and perhaps will, that an action to review the decision to cancel a licence would exist under section 28 of the Federal Court Act in the event that the rules of natural justice are ignored. I am not saying it is certain, but it is possible. The committee felt that the subject should not necessarily be forced to litigation in order to establish his rights or to seek that sort of justice.
Another of the recommendations that we had regarding the carrying on of the work of this committee-really, the first recommendation-was that the criteria, of which I have only dealt with five out of some 17, for scrutiny be written into the Statutory Instruments Act so that they will not need to be adopted and incurred in anew by the two Houses at the commencement of every session of parliament. The committee also suggested that there be an additional criterion, namely, whether a statutory instrument trespasses unduly on the rights and liberties of the subject.
The last point is with regard to our relations with parliament. This answers the question of the cook who was ordered to be boiled in oil. Let it be noted that parliament can do what it wishes within its jurisdiction. It is said it can change a man
March 28, 1977

into a woman, or a woman into a man. But delegated authority must always be subordinate.
"The power to legislate, when delegated by parliament, differs from parliament's own power to legislate. Parliament is supreme and its power to legislate is therefore unlimited. It can do the greatest things; it can do the smallest. It can make general laws ... it can make a particular exception out of them in favour of a particular individual. It can provide ... for the payment of old age pensions to all who fulfill the statutory conditions; it can also provide-and has in fact provided-for boiling the Bishop of Rochester's cook to death. But any power delegated by parliament is necessarily a subordinate power, because it is limited by the terms of the enactment whereby it is delegated."
This is a statement which is undoubtedly written large on the walls of the classrooms when students are dealing with the powers of parliament and delegated authority. It comes from the committee on ministers' powers, better known as the Donoughmore committee, in the United Kingdom in 1932. I think I have now given a satisfactory explanation about the boiling of the cook. Except that the other day there was a debate in this chamber-such debates take place almost every year, and 1 believe one will take place tonight in the Senate- in which great interest was shown in the subject of $1 items.
The co-chairman of my committee, Senator Forsey, has indicated that in a very rare meeting of committee of the whole of the other place the question of $1 items will be raised together with the propriety of some of the things those items set out to do. Perhaps this is the most important battle we shall get into in parliament for a long time, the question of what can be done with $1 items and what can be done with legislation which does not specifically set out the powers which can be used under that legislation. The subject is one which has been well ventilated in this place, and no doubt it will be well ventilated in the other place, so I shall not get into it now.
In the report to both chambers we have dealt with what we consider to be a defect in the method used by parliament to handle delegated legislation. More particularly, we turned to the Statutory Instruments Act. The first point which must be considered as being a defect in the act is the absence of any real system whereby orders which have legislative effect are tabled in the House, are automatically referred to the standing joint committee and are published so that the public may know what is being done. This concerned us because we do not know how many instruments are effectively being hidden from us. We do know, for example, about the guidelines used by the department of immigration. Some of us, more particularly the hon. member for Greenwood, have seen portions of these guidelines. He can advise the House that they do contain substantive rules. We are told, for instance, that they contain a definition of the crime of moral turpitude, the commission of which is a ground for exclusion from Canada. It is our opinion that such rules should not be contained in documents which in no way, shape or form come before a parliamentary committee for scrutiny. This matter is being considered now in connection with the new Immigration Act which is presently before parliament.
The second point with regard to the Statutory Instruments Act is that the definition of a statutory instrument is obscure. I
Statutory Instruments
suppose that if either Senator Forsey or myself operated as strictly as some chairmen are inclined to do, we would be bound to examine each piece of material which comes before us in light of the definition of a statutory instrument under the Statutory Instruments Act and make a ruling as to whether or not the committee was in order in even attempting to examine some of these sacred pronouncements. The fact is that in the end we simply threw up our hands, as did our counsel, in face of the definition set forth in the Statutory Instruments Act. We implore, beseech and beg that when parliament gets around to dealing with the act it gives us a better definition to deal with. The present definition of a regulation is equally obscure, in the opinion of the committee, and as we say in our report at paragraph 45:
There is no provision for a body to give a definitive ruling on whether or not a document is a statutory instrument. There is a procedure by which the Department of Justice can determine whether or not a statutory instrument is a regulation, but this is open to the objection that the parliamentary scrutiny committee is cut off from the decision.
The course which is recommended by the committee-and I must say it is a very non-partisan committee-is to proceed along the lines which were originally recommended by our "father committee", that is, the committee headed by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville, namely, to have one class of document, broadly defined. This would remove the distinction between regulations and statutory instruments. It would subject all documents of the class to uniform procedures as to registration, publication and restriction as to retroactive effect.
The report of the committee headed by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville with regard to what should be the regulation and classification of the documents proposed is set forth in paragraph 47 of the report by Senator Forsey and myself. I simply draw it to the attention of the powers that be in the hope that parliament will have some interest in the problem we are up against and try to help us in our work. We think we have important work to do and we believe, also, that we are hampered by the present unhelpful definition. If nothing else happens immediately, I do hope the Statutory Instruments Act can be implemented so as to include a sensible definition and incorporate criteria to guide us in the examination of these regulations, possibly by way of a schedule to the act.
I have dealt with the recommendations concerning the criteria. I have dealt with the need for a new definition. We also make reference to the enabling powers in the Appropriation Acts, including $1 items. That is paragraph 113 of our report in which we say:
The commiltee endorses the views of the Auditor General. If enabling powers to make statutory instruments are to continue to be granted in Appropriation Acts, the vote texts should be specific and unequivocal, and contain all the wording having legislative effect, with none being contained in the estimates. Legislating by means of dollar votes and altering the purpose of previous votes by a number of successive votes are practices with which the committee does not agree.
May I make a specific point about recommendations dealing with the powers of officers of agricultural agencies. This is a point which did not make much impact when the report was
4386

March 28, 1977
Statutory Instruments
presented the other day, though it was the feeling of the committee that very large and substantial issues are involved here. I could have mentioned these earlier when we dealt with some of the criteria as examples, but I thought I would deal with this specifically at the tail end of my remarks.
It is our opinion that in the past the powers given under agricultural acts to marketing agencies and the like are too broad and sweeping. As a matter of fact, it was said in the committee that we thought ordinary farmers should be treated no worse than ordinary criminals, yet criminals have rights established under the common law and in the Criminal Code which ordinary farmers would probably give some of their eye-teeth to have. For example, here is something which came out in the Saskatchewan hog information, interprovincial and export, regulations. I do not mention this because it is the worst example, but because it was an ordinary example of what one finds under the Agricultural Products Marketing Act. This is one part of the regulations, which is set forth in paragraph 130 of our report:
5(1) Any member or authorized representative of the commission may, at any reasonable time, inspect any place or premises used for the marketing of hogs.
(2) Every person in possession or control of any place or premises referred to in subsection (1) shall
(a)	permit any member or authorized representative of the Commission to inspect such place or premises; and
(b)	furnish any member or authorized representative of the commission with such information in respect of the marketing of hogs as he may reasonably require.
What the regulations do in this case is to give powers of inspection without any requirement that the inspecting officer show his authority or establish his identity. There is no limitation on what is a "reasonable time". The requirement to produce information to an inspector is stronger than that which a peace officer can require of a person. For example, it could destroy, and it does destroy, the inspected person's basic right not to incriminate himself.
These problems have been taken up with the Department of Agriculture and that department is setting to work to remove the objectionable features of many of the regulations pertaining to agricultural marketing. The point should be made that over the years some bad practices had grown up as a result of the actions of people who drew up regulations without there apparently being the scrutiny that we in parliament would have given them had the regulations been presented to us in the first place in the form of legislation.
I think the committee can pat itself on the back for digging out some of these things and starting to effect cures, but it is a long and slow process and sometimes one does not get all the co-operation one would like. Departments, being composed of human beings, as is the committee, are apt to see things in a different light. While mentioning the co-operation of the Department of Agriculture, I am hoping for the co-operation of the Department of Fisheries since some four dozen queries have been directed to that department regarding which the committee has not yet received satisfaction. I should also mention the co-operation that we have enjoyed from both the Privy Council office and from the Minister and Department of

Justice. So gradually I think battles are being won, though there is still an enornous number of battles to be fought.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I make four points of a general philosophic nature in concluding my contribution to this debate. The first is that parliament need not fear the delegation process. I say this because there have been some silly press reactions to the original report of the committee, as though all delegation in itself is necessarily evil. Parliament need not fear the delegation process any more than it need fear its own process of enacting legislation. What we have to fear here is whether the delegation process is properly used. We should also insist that the delegation process be scrutinized properly by the joint committee of which I have the honour to be a chairman. In other words, every member of parliament should take it upon himself to want to know that, when legislation leaves here and is subsequently carried on by a delegated process, that delegated process is exercised properly and examined properly.
Secondly, we must improve our method of dealing with the delegation process. From time to time the House and the other chamber must welcome members of the committee to come and relate our problems, just as I and others are doing. I think possibly there should be a debate at least once a year, or once a session, on the question of how we cope with the delegation process.
Thirdly-I have mentioned this before but it is worth mentioning again-the procedure committee should also take a look at the problem. Perhaps we should be establishing a process whereby all regulations go to the committee most directly affected. For example, regulations under the Agricultural Products Marketing Act should go to the agriculture committee at least once so the members of that committee have an opportunity to discuss them. After all, those members are the most concerned with agricultural matters, much more so than the members of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. They can pronounce more directly on whether the regulations carry out the intention of the legislation and on what they understood to be the intention when that legislation went through.
We do have the advantage in the regulations committee that regulations and statutory instruments are automatically referred to us if passed, I think, since January 1, 1972. Once a regulation properly comes before us, as I understand that most generous reference in section 26 of the Statutory Instruments Act, then it is possible for us to again and again go to the same regulation if we feel it is offensive or should be examined for some reason or another. We never lose our power to examine that particular regulation. The fact is that some of us would feel comfortable if the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry would look at some of the regulations dealing with fisheries, in that they only do so once in a lifetime.
My fourth and final point is that more members and more people from the public should use the process of the committee to look at regulations. If those regulations bother them, they
March 28, 1977

should at least write in and say, "Have you chaps taken a look at this? It seems to affect some of my basic rights. I wonder how you can allow that sort of thing to happen in any part of the parliamentary system."
The purpose of the speech I have just delivered, and the speeches the House has heard from other hon. members, no doubt will give some emphasis to the fact that we are trying to cope with the problems of the delegated process and the fact that we are trying to enlist as many people to this cause as we possibly can.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this second report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, as those who have read it will be able to testify, is a lengthy, complicated, legal document. It is none the worse for that. In effect, it has to be that sort of report dealing with that sort of subject matter. It is important that the salient features may not possibly be recognized because of the torrent of legalistic words. I will bring out some of those features which deserve special consideration.
The committee's primary function is to maintain a watch on the laws made by the delegates of parliament and to subject all rules and regulations to parliamentary scrutiny. I suggest that that delegation is necessary. This delegation is regarded as necessary, as evidenced by the well-known practice of almost all developed countries and their legislatures. There is no way we can rail against delegated legislation and say it should not be: it is here to stay; it is a natural result of the type of society in which we live.
The report which we are now discussing indicates that the intentions of parliament in respect of parliamentary scrutiny have been whittled down by a series of interpretations of the meaning of the expression "rules and statutory instruments" by legalistic refinements of the meaning of these terms. This exercise has apparently been promoted by the Department of Justice. It is not too much to say that the report indicates in great detail how the will of parliament has been frustrated by this process of interpretation by the bureaucracy within the Department of Justice. I am glad the Minister of Justice is going to speak after me. He will be able to correct me if I am wrong, or say wherein the report is wrong.
The interpretation given by the legal advisers of the Privy Council office removes from the class of instruments covered by the act a substantial number of subordinate laws. This is done by the application of what the committee called a magic formula. Unless an enabling power reads that the governor in council or minister may "by order, by rule, by regulation, by warrant, by tariff', and so on, there can be no statutory instruments.
This interpretation would remove, from the class of statutory instruments and the committee's scrutiny, instruments made under enabling powers in common use. For example, the phrase "terms and conditions as the governor in council may prescribe", or "as the board may regulate", do not, in the opinion of the Privy Council, constitute statutory instruments and therefore they are free of regulation.
Statutory Instruments
In this connection I would remind the House that Bill C-24 on immigration which recently received second reading in this House contains much of such phraseology which would remove some of the rules passed by it from the scrutiny of the committee. For example, under section 14 of the new Immigration Act it is provided that where an immigration officer is satisfied that it would not be contrary to this act or the regulations to grant admission to an immigrant who has been authorized to come into Canada, he may, after such further examination as he deems necessary, grant landing to such person and impose terms and conditions of a prescribed nature. That is language which, according to the legal authorities of the Privy Council, means that the rules made in respect of providing or imposing terms and conditions are not to be scrutinized by any instrument of parliament. As far as I can make out, they do not even require publication. That is a secret form of legislating with respect to the rights of people.
The instrument or document describing these terms and conditions for admission would not be a statutory instrument, according to this interpretation, and would not require publication or scrutiny by the committee. To my way of thinking, the legal contortions used to arrive at this extraordinary conclusion are beyond comprehension. It is obvious that they deprive the Regulations and Statutory Instruments Act of the application parliament intended them to have; namely, the committee should have wide jurisdiction over all statutory instruments and legislation. There is no rhyme, no sense or no reason in saying that one parcel of documents should be subject to parliamentary scrutiny and others should not.
To put it another way, an ingenious formula has been found for substantially curtailing the purposes of parliament in passing the act. I know what the purposes were, because I was a member of the MacGuigan committee and I took part in all the debates which dealt with this subject. I believe it was the intention of parliament that this committee should have wide jurisdiction and should not be restricted by these legalistic interpretations which deprive it of much of its jurisdiction. To go into the legal merits of this matter would tax the patience of the House, and indeed I would not even have time to go into them.
The committee said, on page 19 of the report, that despite widespread belief to the contrary, there is no system whereby all orders which have legislative effect and are tabled in parliament are automatically referred to the standing joint committee and are published so that the public can know what is being done. That is the purpose of this, so that the public can know, through the filing and scrutiny of this Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, what is being done to remove an atmosphere of secrecy about laws applicable to Canadian citizens and others in Canada. The committee report continues to read as follows:
There is a system only for regulations and not for all statutory instruments, many of which are effectively hidden, are unpublished or are unknown even to the parliamentary committee.
80010-71V2

March 28, 1977
Statutory Instruments
Because these documents are not said to be statutory instruments, they were not even reported to the committee and the committee did not know that many of them existed-and to this day the committee does not know how many of them exist. The committee recommended the adoption of the definition proposed by the so-called MacGuigan committee which would clear up this question of definition. We hope the government will afford an early opportunity to remedy this situation.
The committee report also refers to the sub-delegation of the rule-making power and suggests that this should be clarified and cut down, and that such delegation should only be allowed when clearly provided for in the legislation. The committee further dealt with the power of dispensing with regulations in favour of individuals and raised many examples where this is being done at present. It was through the exercise of dispensing this power that James II lost his throne and Charles I lost his head. It constitutes a vicious practice designed to ensure that we are governed not by a democratic parliamentary system but by a bureaucracy.
No one in the House does not appreciate the necessity of having a bureaucracy of officials to administer the law, and indeed I think many of us have a good deal of respect for our officials who are serving this country. But to apply a term which I think was originally used in respect of the army and its position vis-a-vis the civilian power, the bureaucracy should be on tap, not on top.
The committee took the view that the wording of the definition section of the act is obscure, and the Privy Council office's interpretation of it is, and I quote the language of the report, "Quixotic in operation and subversive to the committee's function so narrowly to confine the committee as to hamstring it". This parliament is now having a report prepared for it by the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons saying that this provision has hamstrung the committee's functions. I think we should do something about that.
The committee refers to immigration guidelines which the House has been discussing recently in a different context. It says it is satisfied that these guidelines and manuals are in effect statutory instruments and should be disclosed. The committee reports that it has not been vouchsafed either a perusal of the guidelines or the detailed reasons for there not being statutory instruments, and is therefore unable to give an opinion as to whether the guidelines now in existence do, or do not, fall within section 58 of the Immigration Act, or do not lay down any rules applicable to subjects or immigrants.
I invite the House to consider how serious a statement that is. The committee of the House and of the Senate was not even allowed to look at the guidelines which I for one am able to assert dealt with the rules by which we admit people or refuse them admittance to Canada. We were not allowed to even see what these documents are. As they said, they could not judge whether the guidelines now in existence do, or do not, fall within the relevant section of the act.
While it is obvious that the committee cannot pronounce itself on documents it has not seen, these guidelines do contain matters of substance which guide immigration officers' deci-

sions in the case of applicants for immigration into Canada. These documents have been kept rigidly secret, not only from the public or those directly concerned in the cases involved but from parliament as a whole. I hope parliament has enough self-respect to say that this must not continue. The total picture is one, therefore, of frustration and obstruction as well as one of secrecy.
The committee has had before it, as the House knows, another reference to inquire into the secrecy of public documents whose production has been sought in parliament. This committee has not yet reported. I am not quite sure whether it has up to date terms of reference now before it. This refers to a subject that is widely known under the heading of the freedom of information act. This is all part of the same picture in which some of us in the House are striving to bring about greater public participation in the decisions of government. The present report, however, lays the groundwork for some general observations, namely, that we are not governed by participatory democracy, which would require full disclosure of what the government is doing unless the matter falls within a special exemption as clearly set out in the statute.
It is imperative that we should change this situation. Democracy means government by the people. It is essential, for this to be effective, that the people and their representatives should have knowledge. Knowledge, in effect, is power. It can hardly be too much to say that those who have knowledge and power today are the bureaucracy who are supposed to be subordinate. Parliament should take this matter up with vigour and should insist that the definition of regulations and statutory instruments be made broad enough so the committee can function effectively and the Senate and the House of Commons are respected and recognized.
Perhaps we do not need a revolution such as occurred in the days of the Stuart kings of England. But what I think we need is a revolutionary change in attitude, and I hope that when the Minister of Justice speaks in this debate he will say what the government is planning to do to ensure that we move to that freer, more open society in which people have power and in which other instruments of government are in the subordinate position in which they should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the chairman of the committee and the hon. member for Greenwood. As both of them indicated, the matter under discussion, namely, the work of the committee and the report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, is immensely complicated and complex, not only because of the legal technicalities-some of which have been raised this afternoon-but also by reason of the novelty of this area of parliamentary inquiry. Traditionally, in this country, questions as to the legality or not of legislative instruments were left, until the Statutory Instruments Act came into force, to the realm of the courts.
This is the first substantive report by the committee, and as such it merits very careful consideration, as suggested by the
March 28, 1977

hon. co-chairman. I can assure him and the House that the report is receiving careful attention within my department and by the government and that it shall continue to do so.
Because of the importance of the subject 1 accept with readiness and support the suggestion of the co-chairman that some means be found by which this subject could be reviewed, analyzed and debated-if 1 recall the co-chairman's suggestion correctly-on an annual basis so that from time to time we can see the progress which is being made in the area of providing-and this is the desire of hon. members of this House and of the government-that delegated legislation is given proper scrutiny to ensure that this delegation is being done properly.
As the hon. co-chairman indicated, parliament need not fear the delegation process, and as both speakers before me have indicated, that delegation is not new to parliament. It is certainly something which in this complex society and in this complex day we are going to have to continue. And what we as a parliament, and obviously those on this side as members of the administration, must be concerned about is that this delegation is used properly and that we have-on a continuing basis-an adequate process to ensure that its exercise is scrutinized.
The government is as concerned about the scrutiny of subordinate legislation as much as any hon. member in the House and certainly as much as hon. members on the opposition side. I am glad that the hon. co-chairman pointed out the work which preceded the passage of the Statutory Instruments Act, namely, the work of the MacGuigan committee which lead to the passage of the present legislation and the work which hon. members on both sides of the House have done. The hon. co-chairman mentioned a group of people, and he indicated that in any list we invariably leave one out. I would like to add to his list. It was a matter of great interest and concern to the late prime minister Lester B. Pearson that we legislate a proper regime for inspection of statutory instruments. He took particular, personal and keen interest in the work of the MacGuigan committee and the legislation which flowed from it.
I think the process put in place by the Statutory Instruments Act and the standing committee is basically a good one. Our concern here, in what is a new function for parliament-at least, for the Canadian parliament-should be about continually reviewing how the system is working. We should continually be concerned about refining our system as time goes by and bettering the system of scrutiny as our insight and experience increases.
Before dealing with the report, I want to mention one specific matter. While it was not raised by the co-chairman, it was raised by the hon. member for Greenwood. He complained about the definition of statutory instrument-and I also wish to complain about it-but he said that the definition resulted in a whittling down of the matters which could be reviewed by
Statutory Instruments
the committee. He seemed to imply, as some of the speeches in the other place have implied, that there was almost a conspiracy on the part of officials of the Department of Justice to do that. I was pleased to note that later the hon. member indicated in his remarks that he had a very high regard for many of the public servants who serve our country. I am glad he said that, but because of what else has been said in connection with the drawing of regulations I would like to make one point very strongly. Simply stated, I am confident in asserting that the officers of the Privy Council office section of the Department of Justice bring a very high degree of competence and dedication to the very difficult job of examining the myriad of regulatory enactments which pass through their hands. In saying that, I in no way want to take away from the dedication and competence of those in the committee who do exactly the same job.
I would remind hon. members that under the terms of section 3 of the Statutory Instruments Act, all proposed regulations must be inspected by the Department of Justice to ensure that they are authorized by the statute pursuant to which they are made; that they do not constitute an unusual or unexpected use of the authority pursuant to which they are made; that they do not trespass unduly on existing rights and freedoms; and that they are not, in any case, inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of the Canadian Bill of Rights; and the form of draftmanship of the proposed regulations are in accordance with established standards. In carrying out their work as officers in those inspections or in those analyses of matters passed under the Statutory Instruments Act, they are performing duties specified under the Statutory Instruments Act and under section 4 of the Department of Justice Act which provides that the administration of public affairs must be in accordance with the law.
Because of some possible inference by the hon. member for Greenwood and some remarks made in the other place, I want to assure the House that, from my observation, the dedication of the officers of my department to the principle that the administration of public affairs is in accordance with the law, and their dedication to the rule of law, is as strong as that of any member of the committee or any hon. member of this House.
While, obviously, in any free, democratic and parliamentary society it is essential that there be constant vigilance against abuse of public power, in my view this country is undoubtedly fortunate in having law officers of the quality, competence and dedication that it has. While it is fashionable, and always worth a headline, to attack senior civil servants, it has been my experience in four different departments that as a country and as a parliament we are generally well served by this group of dedicated, hard-working and capable advisers.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think from time to time that needs to be said, and I think these advisers are the first to recognize the point I

March 28, 1977
Statutory Instruments
have just made, namely, that in any free society there must be constant vigilance against abuse of public power by those holding public office, elected or otherwise.
As I said in the beginning, this is the first time a committee of parliament has reported on the operations of the Statutory Instruments Act. There is a need for fresh approaches to the problems raised in the report. I want to say that my department and the government as a whole has shown willingness to develop such new approaches.
I would illustrate that claim by example, Mr. Speaker. One problem-dealt with at considerable length in the report, as it should be, because it was a matter of very great concern to the committee-was how to provide the committee with adequate background information to the regulations it was examining while at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the advice provided by my department to its client departments and to the government generally. This protection is akin to that provided by the solicitor-client privilege at common law. The hon. member for Peace River might note-and I see him taking notes-that I believe even he recognizes the confidentiality of legal advice. I do not want to quote Hansard, but when he was a parliamentary secretary on another occasion he made a very long speech about it. He also included an exemption for legal advice covering this type of material in the right to information bill that he introduced in the last session of parliament.
On the one hand there is the question of protecting the legal advice given by my department to the government, and on the other the valid and legitimate need of the committee to have more information about the regulations they are scrutinizing. A solution was developed to this problem which hinges upon the distinction between legal advice and statements by the relevant departments as to their legal and policy position vis-a-vis the particular regulation in question. As a result of meeting with the committee and discussing this matter at length, I made a series of recommendations to my colleagues in cabinet who agreed-and the committee has been subsequently so informed-that henceforth each department shall have a senior adviser designated to provide these statements. My deputy minister has written to other deputies to inform them of this new arrangement. Each department will have a senior officer who will provide these legal and policy statements to the committee upon request.
I would hope that when the question of legal advice and the need of the committee for information arises the arrangement we have proposed will serve both those needs and interests. I am happy that the committee notes these new arrangements in its report and expresses the hope that they will serve the committee's purpose. I join in that hope.
It has been mentioned that this is a very legalistic and technical report. I should like to deal, in order, with some of the other sections of the report, and this discussion will as a result become somewhat complicated. I think it is necessary, however, that I put some observations on the record. This
being an extensive report covering many areas of the subject, I would hope that members of the committee would not want me to respond today with a speech to cover every paragraph. Hon. members are having some difficulty keeping awake at the present time, and they certainly would be sound asleep if I dealt with every paragraph of the report, as it raises many, many issues.
I would like to begin with Sections D and F of the report which deal with the form and public availability of statutory instruments. With regard to the form of statutory instruments, the committee's basic concern relates to the citation of the statutory authority for each instrument, the citation of previously relevant amendments and the publication of explanatory notes. When they conduct their inspection of each statutory instrument, the Privy Council office section of the Department of Justice will normally see that the relevant statutory authority is not only legally valid but that it is also cited. Henceforth, this long-standing administrative practice will be refined to as great an extent as possible to ensure that the circumstances referred to by the committee will become even more rare. 1 think the co-chairman acknowledged that progress was already being made in this area.
The matter of providing appropriate footnote referencing to the latest relevant amendments to instruments is now being looked into by the Privy Council office, as is the matter of publication of explanatory notes. I can only state at the present time that the clerk of the Privy Council is considering the committee's recommendations very seriously, and I hope very shortly to be able to inform committee members of new developments in this regard.
I should like to turn now to section E of the report which concerns alleged defects in the Statutory Instruments Act and which has been the subject of comments by the hon. member for Greenwood. The co-chairman of the committee has also made a number of recommendations in this regard which principally, but not entirely, relate to the definition of "statutory instrument" in the act. The committee says it has found this definition incomprehensible and unworkable. In response to that, I say that basically I have sympathy with them on this point and, as I indicated when I appeared before the committee, my officials and I are prepared to consider any specific suggestions the committee might wish to make toward improving the definition. The committee has recommended the inclusion of certain departmental guidelines, directives and manuals-a recommendation which I have raised in correspondence with the committee and the relevant departments.
The committee also recommended that a new definition of a statutory instrument should be arrived at "by taking the sum of the law-making exercised by the Crown and its agencies and any other delegate or subdelegate of parliament and where made pursuant to or under a statute or to the prerogative and by declaring the whole to be subject to parliamentary scrutiny." This would, however, cause some problems of interpretation just as does the present definition. While I think the need for some exemption to this definition was dealt with in the committee's report, it would seem to me, touching only on

March 28, 1977

certain matters, that such a general definition would, subject to whatever exemptions existed, include all bylaws made by private corporations established by an act of parliament, copies of every order made by a judicial or quasi-judicial body established by act of parliament, plus the ordinances of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and any regulations or orders made thereunder.
The value or even the wisdom of having a committee of the federal parliament reviewing this kind of material seems somewhat questionable to me. There is a need for a better definition of statutory instrument and a need to avoid some of the problems created by the present definition. And, as was said, my officials and I are considering the observations made in the report. And, I say that to indicate that in the light of difficulties with regard to the definition, I would still consider any further observations emanating from members of the committee or the committee itself. These would help in the formulation of a precise definition which may be proposed as a change to the Statutory Instruments Act.
The hon. member for Greenwood said he hopes the government will provide an early opportunity for dealing with this question in parliament. I assure him that my officials and I are considering the observations of the committee in its report but, as the hon. member knows, the timing of the introduction of any amendments to the act is not in my hands. It is entirely out of my hands in that it is a matter for the President of the Privy Council and the government as a whole. One appreciates that the legislative list with which this parliament must deal is extensive.
The committee also recommends that the Statutory Instruments Act should be amended so that as a general rule no subordinate legislation should come into effect before it is published. The previous speaker also raised the problem of publication. The Statutory Instruments Act at present already effectively deals with this point in a slightly different manner. Subsection 11(2) provides that, with certain specific exceptions, no person shall be convicted of an offence consisting of a contravention of any regulation that at the time of the alleged contravention was not published in the Canada Gazette in both official languages.
The subsection makes a sensible exception in most cases where it is proved that at the date of the alleged contravention reasonable steps had been taken to bring the purport of the regulation to the notice of those persons likely to be affected by it. For example, there are occasions when it is necessary to act quickly, such as at the close of a fishing season for conservation purposes. This happens in my part of the country weekly, sometimes almost daily. In such cases signs are posted immediately near the river or lake affected, which would seem to be a better method of informing the concerned parties than publication in the Canada Gazette, which I do not think is a best-seller among fishermen. If the government waited for publication in the Gazette, the purpose of the closing would be lost.
Statutory Instruments
The committee also recommends that all subordinate legislation, unless expressly excepted by the terms of the Statutory Instruments Act, should be registered, published and transmitted to the committee. The act, however, already requires all regulations to be transmitted to the clerk of the Privy Council for registration. Furthermore, it provides as a general rule that no regulation shall come into force before registration. It also requires publication in the Canada Gazette after registration.
Finally, with regard to transmission of regulations to the committee, my understanding is that directives already exist on this point. Steps will be taken to ensure that this is indeed the case already prior to the introduction of, say, amendments to the act. In effect, with respect to regulations the committee's recommendation is already being implemented. The further recommendation that these requirements should extend to all subordinate legislation as defined by the committee may cause severe difficulties. One need only again mention court orders and ordinances of the territorial councils to give hon. members some idea of these difficulties. This issue is one which will be receiving further attention from appropriate officials.
The committee also recommends that "the Statutory Instruments Act should provide for a statutory instruments reference committee having the authority to issue a conclusive determination for the purposes of parliamentary scrutiny as to whether any particular document is a statutory instrument or not." The effect of this recommendation would be to delegate to the proposed reference committee the determination of the term "statutory instrument", as I understand the recommendation, for all the purposes of the act and not just for the purpose of scrutiny by the standing joint committee.
Personally, I have some difficulty with assigning to a committee of the House the task of defining words in a statute. Hopefully, an improvement of the definition would make such a recommendation unnecessary. An improved definition could also handle one other recommendation of the committee, namely, that any departmental guidelines, directives or manuals which contain substantive rules not contained in statutes should be included in the definition of "statutory instruments" and subject to parliamentary scrutiny. It seems to me, unless I misread the report, that if these difficulties could be dealt with by way of definition, we should not need some of the other recommendations. I am glad to note that the co-chairman seems to indicate that I have read the report correctly.
1 apologize for being so technical, Mr. Speaker, but I think the members of the committee would wish me to deal fully with their report. Recommendation 10 of the summary, in section E of the report, advocates that the committee should be provided with reasons wherever any statutory instrument is to come into force before registration and publication. This strikes me as an extremely reasonable proposal and I am pleased to announce that steps will be taken to implement it. The government agrees, as well, with the next recommendation of the committee, namely, that the words "regulation-making authority" should be redefined. The objective here is to make it clear that these words mean the department, ministry or

March 28, 1977
Statutory Instruments
other body which recommends the regulations to the governor in council.
The final recommendtion of the committee with respect to the Statutory Instruments Act is that section 32 should be amended to require the publication of regulations registered under that section. With few exceptions, the publication of these regulations has now been carried out. I think the committee in its report mentions, for example, among the remainder which have not been published, regulations which govern the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. With respect to all of these, the Department of Justice will publish this summer a complete consolidation including all regulations and other statutory instruments enacted since 1955. This consolidation would include all regulations registered under section 32, which will give effect in practice to the recommendation of the committee.
In section H of the report the committee recommends that any subdelegation of rule-making powers should be expressly spelled out in the establishing statute. This recommendation, like many of those in the report, raises what is essentially a fine question of law involving the extent of the authority granted by the general words which are traditionally employed when conferring regulation-making powers. After considerable research and consideration of the matter, Professor E. A. Driedger, Q.C., a well known Canadian authority on legislation, has concluded that the results of the court decisions to date "would appear to be that there is no rule or presumption for or against subdelegation and that in each case it is a question of interpretation of the language of the particular statute". The committee rejects this conclusion and I suggest one can only await the final decision of the courts on this matter.
With regard, however, to the general question of the desirability of subdelegation, it should be noted that the combination of the complexity of contemporary regulations and the need for flexibility in applying them in the field has created what is, indeed, an inescapable need for subdelegation as discussed in this section and sections I, J and K of the report. In my discussion of these sections I will attempt to demonstrate this necessity. In section I of the report the committee deals with the language of delegation. My officials are now studying, for future use, the general recommendations contained therein. Hopefully, hon. members will bear the committee's recommendations in mind in enacting forthcoming legislation. It should be noted, however, that it would not be desirable to impose a straitjacket on the words used in legislation by forbidding, as the committee recommends, the use of particular terms such as "respecting".
Section K of the report concerns enabling powers which are granted by the use of Appropriation Acts, the so-called "dollar items". This was a topic of considerable debate and a ruling by you, Mr. Speaker, last week. I do not intend to repeat all that was said at that time. I follow the example of the co-chairman who moved the motion before us today. One can understand
the concern which was debated last week to which Your Honour's ruling adds a new perspective. I will leave it simply to the debate that was held last week and to the effect of the ruling of Your Honour with regard to that matter.
Section S of the report deals with the power of officers of agricultural agencies. In this regard I would like, first of all, to state that, as the committee itself points out, the regulations setting out the powers of officers of agricultural agencies are within the terms of the acts of parliament governing these matters. Second, I should point out that there does not seem to be evidence that agricultural agencies are presently trampling on the civil liberties of citizens. As the committee has recognized, the Department of Agriculture has co-operated willingly in removing objectionable features of regulations when these have been brought to its attention.
I would like now to turn to a section of the report which I understand has given rise to a fair amount of controversy amongst the members of the committee. It was touched upon by the hon. member for Greenwood. A good portion of the committee's report deals with regulations that exempt one or more individuals from the application of general regulations. Part J of the report gives examples of such regulations, and appendix III of the report sets out at considerable length why the committee considers such regulations to be illegal.
It is the committee's opinion that such regulations have been outlawed by the "revolutionary settlement" embodied in the English bill of rights of 1689. The report sets out the history surrounding the passage of the act in Britain and concludes, in essence, that the so-called "dispensing regulations" cannot validly be made unless each and every case is expressly authorized in the body of the statute itself. This particular matter was mentioned by the hon. member for Greenwood and my name has been linked with those who in times past have "lost their heads" over the issue. I have read speeches made in the other place by the co-chairman from that place wishing to give me the title "latter-day Stuart"-a title which I reject.

speechtext: Maybe you are a Latter Day Saint.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This would seem to be an issue which, in the final instance, involves a subtle point of statutory interpretation. It is not extraordinary that there is disagreement between the lawyers on the committee and those of the Department of Justice as to the interpretation of the sections which provide for the creation of regulations. Justice's view is simply that all the regulation-making powers in question include the power to limit the application of the regulations. Since the regulationmaking power is itself a parliamentary enactment, the "revolutionary settlement" principle is not infringed upon.
The report also indicates, in section N, the committee's disagreement with the practice of departing from the language of the statutes when the same idea is repeated in the instruments made thereunder. On the very few occasions where this has occurred, the responsible departments acknowledged that it was not a proper practice. Certainly, the officers in the Department of Justice will endeavour to assist the committee
[Mr. Basford.J
March 28, 1977

by ensuring that such instances do not occur, or are corrected if they do occur.
In section O of the report the committee indicates that the statutory conditions precedent to the making of published instruments should be recounted in the preamble as having been complied with. The committee has noted, however, that the legal advisers to the Privy Council office have co-operated with it in this regard and they, undoubtedly, will continue to do so in future. The report raises many other technical points which, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, are too numerous to cover here. In conclusion, I would simply like to state that the Department of Justice and the government will continue to examine the good work of the committee in what, as was also said before, is a new area of parliamentary activity, scrutiny and reporting.
It should be noted that there have been occasions where the legal views of the committee have been brought to the attention of justice officers who have agreed, and have subsequently recommended to the departments that the regulations in question be amended.
I agree with the comments of the co-chairman that we must always ensure that there is in place an effective means of scrutiny, and that we in parliament as much as within government itself, have two jobs, namely to ensure that our regulations are properly written and properly passed. We also have to ensure that the committee gets the kind of information, support and help it needs to do its job properly. We should not rely upon the courts to ensure that our regulations are properly passed. We should not rely upon the hope that if a regulation is not properly passed, some citizen will take it to court and challenge it. It is our responsibility to put into place both the proper governmental and parliamentary processes and procedures.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would indicate that I have about one minute left. I was making the point that while we have to ensure that we always have in place appropriate governmental processes and parliamentary procedures to ensure that our regulations are proper and that we should not rely upon citizens having to go to court to exercise their right and have the court declare regulations ultra vires. However, it is significant that almost every regulation passed by the government affects a citizen in some way, some corporation in some way, or some association in some way.
A search of the court proceedings of this country would indicate that though from time to time particular regulations are knocked out by the courts, these are very rare occasions indeed. I believe that on the whole we can take some comfort from the fact that the processes within government and within
Statutory Instruments
parliament have ensured that only very few regulations are challenged in the courts. This perspective is important when our attention turns, as it undoubtedly will from time to time, to cases where there has been a mistake.

Then there is the application of those orders in council. My learned friend from Halifax-East Hants, the co-chairman of the committee, has stated that parliament is supreme.
